text: Open-source Geographic Information System QGIS1 was used to clean and prepare the data, which was then input into a commercial specialized 3D modeling software package, Leapfrog Geo2, to construct the initial geologic framework. The overall project workflow, from literature review to data collection and model construction, is summarized in Figure 8. This model was subsequently refined by integrating additional geologic information related to various units. This comprehensive approach facilitated the identification of promising sites for detailed investigation, assessing the geologic suitability of preselected locations, and the initiation of techno-economic analyses for specific geothermal cooling technologies. 1 QGIS Development Team (3.28.6). Project workflow for geothermal 3D modeling 2.2.1 3D Geologic Model The development of a 3D geologic model for the SJMA began with an in-depth review of relevant literature and the compilation of geologic, hydrogeologic, and geospatial datasets. Prior to integrating with the modeling software, these datasets underwent extensive preprocessing to ensure compatibility and consistency. Key steps included extracting and converting well locations to the appropriate coordinate reference system, digitizing well logs into formats compatible with commercial modeling tools, and georeferencing legacy cross sections and maps. Additional tasks involved reprojecting both vector and raster datasets as well as merging and simplifying digital geologic maps to create a unified framework. All spatial data were projected using the WGS 84 UTM Zone 19N coordinate reference system, with units in meters. The final 3D geologic and geothermal conceptual models incorporated a diverse array of data sources, including topographic and bathymetric surfaces, geologic cross sections, formation top and thickness contour maps, well logs, and geologic maps (Table 2). 14 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies at www.nlr.gov/publications. The full extent of the model was well developed; however, surficial deposits, due to their complex and heterogeneous nature, were not included in the initial model. To address this limitation, a secondary 3D model was generated by clipping the original model to the area defined by the black inset box labeled “San Juan Metropolitan Area,” where the modeling of surficial sediments can be handled with greater resolution and accuracy (Figure 9).
